paragraphs.text: Stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis with neurologic defects (SDCHCN) is a rare form of stomatocytosis. It is associated with a cold-induced red cell cation leak, hemolytic anemia and hepatosplenomegaly, together with cataracts, seizures, mental retardation and movement disorder (Flatt et al., 2011). Flatt et al. (2011) showed that the disorder results from mutations in the SLC2A1 gene, which encodes the GLUT1 glucose transporter. They considered it a novel form of GLUT1 deficiency syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Bawazir et al. (2012) described an infant with GLUT1 deficiency and a cation-leaky red cell state. The infant presented with erratic hyperkalemia, neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, anemia, hepatic dysfunction and microcephaly, and later developed seizures and delayed developmental milestones. MRI and CT of the brain showed multiple abnormalities, including periventricular calcification. Vision was impaired because of both cataracts and retinal dysfunction.

paragraphs.text: Lande et al. (1982) used 1-dimensional SDS gel electrophoresis to separate the erythrocyte membrane band 7 proteins into components of about 30, 28 and 26 kD. The 28-kD component was decreased in both of their patients. Two-dimensional electrophoresis split the normal 28-kD component into 2 proteins, 22 x 8 and 60 x 8. In the patients with hereditary stomatocytosis and cryohydrocytosis, protein 22 x 8 was completely absent, whereas 60 x 8 was present as usual. All band 7 proteins, including 22 x 8, were invariably present in normal subjects and in reticulocytosis controls.

paragraphs.text: Fricke et al. (2004) studied 3 new isolated cases and 1 new pedigree of hereditary stomatocytosis, and expanded on 1 previously reported case. Western blotting of red cell membranes showed deficiency of the 32-kD membrane protein stomatin in all cases. All cases had pronounced cation leaks at 37 degrees C, with markedly abnormal intracellular Na+ and K+ concentrations. Immunocytochemistry showed that the stomatin deficiency was not complete. On blood films, some red cells were stomatin-positive and most were negative, although in 1 case only a minority were negative. All platelets and neutrophils were stomatin-positive.

paragraphs.text: Among their cases of stomatin-deficient hereditary stomatocytosis, Fricke et al. (2004) found marked differences in how the passive K+ leak depended on temperature. Three cases showed a simple monotonic temperature dependence. Two cases showed a minimum at about 20 to 25 degrees C, so that the cells were extremely leaky at 0 degrees C; this is the phenotype known as cryohydrocytosis. Fricke et al. (2004) associated this stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis variant with neurologic dysfunction.

paragraphs.text: Bawazir et al. (2012) described an infant with stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis with neurologic defects. The infant had erratic pseudohyperkalemia, neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, anemia, hepatic dysfunction, microcephaly, seizures, developmental delay, periventricular calcification, cataracts and retinal dysfunction. In this patient, Bawazir et al. (2012) identified a trinucleotide deletion in the SLC2A1 gene that deletes isoleucine 435 or 436 of GLUT1. The patient's red cells were extremely leaky to cations and lost potassium in a temperature-dependent way.
